Neonates of the Diamond stingray (Hypanus dipterurus) emerge from their mothers as fully formed, free-swimming pups with a total length at birth typically spanning 19 to 28 cm (19-28 cm) [Lb = 19-28 cm], a range that reflects the considerable investment in yolk-dependent embryonic development. The gestation period, which culminates in parturition at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], has been estimated to last approximately 9 months [ab = approximately 9 months], a duration that aligns with the slow metabolic pace characteristic of many batoids. This comparatively extended intrauterine phase allows pups to attain a relatively large size at birth, which likely confers a survival advantage by reducing vulnerability to gape-limited predators during the critical transition to independent foraging. Field observations indicate that newly born individuals, or pups, immediately commence active feeding on small benthic crustaceans, with the first exogenous feeding occurring mere days after parturition. This range in neonatal length (19-28 cm) [Lb = 19-28 cm] underscores a life-history strategy favoring high neonatal investment over high fecundity.

Growth trajectories for this species exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining considerably larger body dimensions than their male counterparts. The ultimate disc width, representing the asymptotic size achieved after growth plateaus, has been recorded at 92.4 cm [Li = 92.4 cm] for adult females, a value that positions H. dipterurus among the larger members of the Dasyatidae family. Male ultimate disc width, in contrast, is considerably smaller at 62.2 cm [Li = 62.2 cm], a difference that likely reflects distinct selective pressures associated with reproductive roles and the energetic demands of gestation in females. This pattern of size dimorphism is consistent with that observed in many dasyatid rays, where females must accommodate developing embryos within the uterine environment. The substantial disparity in maximal size between the sexes, with females exceeding males by roughly 30 cm in disc width, also influences the disc width at which sexual maturation occurs.

Puberty in Diamond stingray is tightly linked to body size rather than strictly to age, with individuals undergoing the onset of gametogenesis and reproductive activation upon reaching a critical morphological threshold. For the population as a whole, the disc width at puberty is 57.3 cm [Lp = 57.3 cm], a value that likely reflects the energetic requirement to allocate resources toward both continuing somatic growth and incipient reproductive function. Males, however, reach sexual maturity at a considerably smaller body size, with a disc width at puberty of 46.5 cm [Lp = 46.5 cm], a pattern that is common among elasmobranchs where males engage in reproductive activity earlier and at a smaller size than females. This divergence in maturation size is directly linked to the different energetic investments each sex must make: males need only produce sperm and locate mates, whereas females must eventually support the substantial cost of gestation. The date for the onset of maturity in males is thus attained earlier in the lifespan, allowing them more opportunities to mate across multiple seasons.

Reproductive output in the Diamond stingray is modest but consistent, reflecting a strategy of producing a small number of relatively large offspring. Females typically bear a litter size of 1 to 3 pups [N_R_i = a litter size of 1 to 3 pups], with the most frequently observed count being two pups per reproductive event. This low fecundity per event is offset by a regular annual reproductive cycle, as most females are assumed to produce approximately 2 litters each year [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters each year] under the prevailing thermal conditions of their habitat, which average 14.9 °C [T = 14.9 °C]. The combination of one to three pups per litter with approximately two litters each year yields a relatively slow population turnover rate, characteristic of a K-selected life-history strategy. The maximum adult body mass attainable by females has been estimated at 32,100 grams [Wwi = 32,100 grams], a value derived from a length-weight relationship and reflecting the considerable size of the largest, reproductively senescent individuals. This substantial body mass supports both the energetic cost of gestation and the annual production of 1 to 3 pups [Ri = annual production of 1 to 3 pups].

This maximum recorded lifespan is achieved under the typical environmental temperature regime of 14.9 °C [T = 14.9 °C], a thermal context that contributes to the species' slow metabolic rate and gradual accumulation of somatic damage. The combination of late maturity, modest reproductive output, and extended lifespan aligns with a conservative life-history strategy, common among large elasmobranchs that occupy stable, predictable environments. The oldest documented individuals are typically large females that have ceased reproductive activity, having exhausted their finite pool of ovarian follicles. This post-reproductive phase of life, though brief, may play a role in population dynamics by allowing experienced individuals to serve as spatial anchors for social aggregations.
